solution: By definition \(P(E|F) = \frac{P(E \cap F)}{P(F)}\) and \(P(F|E) = \frac{P(E \cap F)}{P(E)}\). Here \(P(E \cap F) = 0.2\), \(P(F) = 0.3\), \(P(E) = 0.6\). So \(P(E|F) = \frac{0.2}{0.3} = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(P(F|E) = \frac{0.2}{0.6} = \frac{1}{3}\). Hence \(P(E|F) = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(P(F|E) = \frac{1}{3}\).

From \(P(B|A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}\) we get \(P(A \cap B) = P(B|A)\,P(A)\). Substituting \(P(B|A) = 0.4\) and \(P(A) = 0.8\), \(P(A \cap B) = 0.4 \times 0.8 = 0.32\). Hence \(P(A \cap B) = 0.32\).
Here \(P(A \cap B) = P(B|A)\,P(A) = 0.4 \times 0.8 = 0.32\). By the addition theorem \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = 0.8 + 0.5 - 0.32 = 0.98\). Hence \(P(A \cup B) = 0.98\).

From \(2P(A) = P(B) = \frac{5}{13}\) we get \(P(B) = \frac{5}{13}\) and \(P(A) = \frac{5}{26}\). Since \(P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\), \(P(A \cap B) = \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{5}{13} = \frac{2}{13}\). Then \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \frac{5}{26} + \frac{10}{26} - \frac{4}{26} = \frac{11}{26}\). Hence \(P(A \cup B) = \frac{11}{26}\).
By the addition theorem \(P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) = \frac{6}{11} + \frac{5}{11} - \frac{7}{11} = \frac{4}{11}\). Hence \(P(A \cap B) = \frac{4}{11}\).

First \(P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) = \frac{6}{11} + \frac{5}{11} - \frac{7}{11} = \frac{4}{11}\). Then \(P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{4/11}{5/11} = \frac{4}{5}\). Hence \(P(A|B) = \frac{4}{5}\).
As above \(P(A \cap B) = \frac{6}{11} + \frac{5}{11} - \frac{7}{11} = \frac{4}{11}\). Then \(P(B|A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)} = \frac{4/11}{6/11} = \frac{2}{3}\). Hence \(P(B|A) = \frac{2}{3}\).

The sample space for three tosses has \(8\) equally likely outcomes: \(HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT\). Here \(F = \{HHH, HHT\}\), so \(P(F) = \frac{2}{8}\). The event \(E \cap F\) means heads on the first two tosses and a head on the third, i.e. \(\{HHH\}\), so \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{1}{8}\). Therefore \(P(E|F) = \frac{1/8}{2/8} = \frac{1}{2}\). Hence \(P(E|F) = \frac{1}{2}\).

Out of the \(8\) equally likely outcomes, \(E\) (at least two heads) \(= \{HHH, HHT, HTH, THH\}\) and \(F\) (at most two heads) is everything except \(HHH\), so \(F\) has \(7\) outcomes and \(P(F) = \frac{7}{8}\). Then \(E \cap F = \{HHT, HTH, THH\}\), giving \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{3}{8}\). Therefore \(P(E|F) = \frac{3/8}{7/8} = \frac{3}{7}\). Hence \(P(E|F) = \frac{3}{7}\).

Of the \(8\) equally likely outcomes, \(E\) (at most two tails) excludes only \(TTT\), so \(E\) has \(7\) outcomes; \(F\) (at least one tail) excludes only \(HHH\), so \(P(F) = \frac{7}{8}\). An outcome lies in \(E \cap F\) when it has one or two tails, i.e. \(\{HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH\}\), so \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{6}{8}\). Therefore \(P(E|F) = \frac{6/8}{7/8} = \frac{6}{7}\). Hence \(P(E|F) = \frac{6}{7}\).

The sample space is \(\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}\), each outcome with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). The event \(E\), a tail on one coin, is \(\{HT, TH\}\) and the event \(F\), one coin shows a head, is also \(\{HT, TH\}\). So \(P(F) = \frac{2}{4}\) and \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{2}{4}\), giving \(P(E|F) = \frac{2/4}{2/4} = 1\). Hence \(P(E|F) = 1\).

With sample space \(\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}\), the event \(E\) (no tail) is \(\{HH\}\) and \(F\) (no head) is \(\{TT\}\), so \(P(F) = \frac{1}{4}\). These are disjoint, so \(E \cap F = \phi\) and \(P(E \cap F) = 0\). Therefore \(P(E|F) = \frac{0}{1/4} = 0\). Hence \(P(E|F) = 0\).

Three throws of a die give \(6^3 = 216\) equally likely outcomes. The event \(F\), a \(6\) then a \(5\) on the first two throws, is \(\{(6,5,x) : x = 1,2,\dots,6\}\), so \(P(F) = \frac{6}{216}\). The event \(E \cap F\) is the single outcome \((6,5,4)\), so \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{1}{216}\). Therefore \(P(E|F) = \frac{1/216}{6/216} = \frac{1}{6}\). Hence \(P(E|F) = \frac{1}{6}\).

Writing \(M\), \(F\), \(S\) for mother, father and son, the sample space of line-ups has \(3! = 6\) equally likely arrangements. The event \(F\), father in the middle, is \(\{MFS, SFM\}\), so \(P(F) = \frac{2}{6}\). In both of these the son stands at an end, so \(E \cap F = \{MFS, SFM\}\) and \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{2}{6}\). Therefore \(P(E|F) = \frac{2/6}{2/6} = 1\). Hence \(P(E|F) = 1\).

Rolling two distinguishable dice gives \(36\) equally likely ordered pairs (black, red). The conditioning event \(F\), black die shows \(5\), is \(\{(5,1),(5,2),(5,3),(5,4),(5,5),(5,6)\}\), so \(P(F) = \frac{6}{36}\). Among these the sum exceeds \(9\) only for \((5,5)\) and \((5,6)\), so \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{2}{36}\). Therefore the required probability is \(\frac{2/36}{6/36} = \frac{1}{3}\). Hence the conditional probability is \(\frac{1}{3}\).

Of the \(36\) equally likely ordered pairs (black, red), the conditioning event \(F\), red die less than \(4\), has red \(\in \{1,2,3\}\) and black anything, so it contains \(3 \times 6 = 18\) outcomes and \(P(F) = \frac{18}{36}\). A sum of \(8\) with red \(\in \{1,2,3\}\) needs black \(= 8 - \text{red}\), which is \(7\) (impossible), \(6\), \(5\); so \(E \cap F = \{(6,2),(5,3)\}\) and \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{2}{36}\). Therefore the required probability is \(\frac{2/36}{18/36} = \frac{1}{9}\). Hence the conditional probability is \(\frac{1}{9}\).

The sample space is \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) with each outcome of probability \(\frac{1}{6}\), so \(P(E) = \frac{3}{6}\), \(P(F) = \frac{2}{6}\) and \(E \cap F = \{3\}\) gives \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{1}{6}\). Then \(P(E|F) = \frac{1/6}{2/6} = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(P(F|E) = \frac{1/6}{3/6} = \frac{1}{3}\). Hence \(P(E|F) = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(P(F|E) = \frac{1}{3}\).

Here \(E \cup F = \{1,2,3,5\}\), so \((E \cup F) \cap G = \{2,3,5\}\) and \(P((E \cup F) \cap G) = \frac{3}{6}\); also \(E \cap F = \{3\}\), so \((E \cap F) \cap G = \{3\}\) and \(P((E \cap F) \cap G) = \frac{1}{6}\). With \(P(G) = \frac{4}{6}\), \(P((E \cup F)|G) = \frac{3/6}{4/6} = \frac{3}{4}\) and \(P((E \cap F)|G) = \frac{1/6}{4/6} = \frac{1}{4}\). Hence \(P((E \cup F)|G) = \frac{3}{4}\) and \(P((E \cap F)|G) = \frac{1}{4}\).

Writing each outcome as (elder, younger), the sample space is \(\{(b,b),(b,g),(g,b),(g,g)\}\), all equally likely. (i) The event that the youngest is a girl is \(\{(b,g),(g,g)\}\), of probability \(\frac{2}{4}\), and both girls is \(\{(g,g)\}\), of probability \(\frac{1}{4}\); so the conditional probability is \(\frac{1/4}{2/4} = \frac{1}{2}\). (ii) The event that at least one is a girl is \(\{(b,g),(g,b),(g,g)\}\), of probability \(\frac{3}{4}\); so the conditional probability is \(\frac{1/4}{3/4} = \frac{1}{3}\). Hence the answers are \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{3}\).

The bank holds \(300 + 200 + 500 + 400 = 1400\) questions. Let \(E\) be 'easy' and \(M\) be 'multiple choice'. The multiple choice questions number \(500 + 400 = 900\), so \(P(M) = \frac{900}{1400}\), and the easy multiple choice questions number \(500\), so \(P(E \cap M) = \frac{500}{1400}\). Then \(P(E|M) = \frac{500/1400}{900/1400} = \frac{5}{9}\). Hence the required probability is \(\frac{5}{9}\).

Throwing two dice gives \(36\) equally likely ordered pairs. The conditioning event \(F\), the two numbers are different, excludes the \(6\) doublets, so it has \(30\) outcomes and \(P(F) = \frac{30}{36}\). The pairs with sum \(4\) are \((1,3), (2,2), (3,1)\), of which only \((1,3)\) and \((3,1)\) have different numbers, so \(P(E \cap F) = \frac{2}{36}\). Then \(P(E|F) = \frac{2/36}{30/36} = \frac{1}{15}\). Hence the required probability is \(\frac{1}{15}\).

The first throw gives a multiple of \(3\) only for \(3\) or \(6\), in which case the die is thrown again; otherwise a coin is tossed. So the sample space is \(\{(3,1),\dots,(3,6),(6,1),\dots,(6,6)\}\) each of probability \(\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{36}\), together with \(\{(1,H),(1,T),(2,H),(2,T),(4,H),(4,T),(5,H),(5,T)\}\) each of probability \(\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{12}\). Let \(E\) be 'the coin shows a tail' and \(F\) be 'at least one die shows a \(3\)'. Then \(F = \{(3,1),(3,2),(3,3),(3,4),(3,5),(3,6),(6,3)\}\), so \(P(F) = \frac{7}{36}\). Every outcome of \(F\) involves two throws of the die and no coin toss, while every outcome of \(E\) involves a coin toss, so \(E \cap F = \phi\) and \(P(E \cap F) = 0\). Therefore \(P(E|F) = \frac{0}{7/36} = 0\). Hence the required probability is \(0\).

Let \(A\) be 'the first card is black' and \(B\) be 'the second card is black'. The pack has \(26\) black cards out of \(52\), so \(P(A) = \frac{26}{52} = \frac{1}{2}\). Since the first card is not replaced, \(25\) black cards remain among \(51\), so \(P(B|A) = \frac{25}{51}\). By the multiplication theorem \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B|A) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{25}{51} = \frac{25}{102}\). Hence the probability that both cards are black is \(\frac{25}{102}\).

The box is approved exactly when all three oranges drawn (without replacement) are good. Of \(15\) oranges \(12\) are good, so by the multiplication theorem the probability is \(\frac{12}{15} \times \frac{11}{14} \times \frac{10}{13} = \frac{1320}{2730} = \frac{44}{91}\). Hence the probability that the box is approved for sale is \(\frac{44}{91}\).

Let \(H\) be 'reads Hindi' and \(E\) be 'reads English', so \(P(H) = 0.6\), \(P(E) = 0.4\) and \(P(H \cap E) = 0.2\). Then \(P(H \cup E) = 0.6 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.8\), and reading neither is the complement of this: \(1 - 0.8 = 0.2\). Hence the required probability is \(0.2 = \frac{1}{5}\).

With \(H\) 'reads Hindi' and \(E\) 'reads English', \(P(H) = 0.6\) and \(P(H \cap E) = 0.2\). The required probability is \(P(E|H) = \frac{P(H \cap E)}{P(H)} = \frac{0.2}{0.6} = \frac{1}{3}\). Hence the required probability is \(\frac{1}{3}\).

With \(H\) 'reads Hindi' and \(E\) 'reads English', \(P(E) = 0.4\) and \(P(H \cap E) = 0.2\). The required probability is \(P(H|E) = \frac{P(H \cap E)}{P(E)} = \frac{0.2}{0.4} = \frac{1}{2}\). Hence the required probability is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Let \(R_1\) and \(B_1\) be the events that the first ball drawn is red and black; each has probability \(\frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}\). The ball is returned and \(2\) more of its colour are added, so before the second draw the urn holds \(12\) balls: \(7\) red and \(5\) black if the first was red, and \(5\) red and \(7\) black if the first was black. Thus \(P(R_2|R_1) = \frac{7}{12}\) and \(P(R_2|B_1) = \frac{5}{12}\). By the theorem of total probability, \(P(R_2) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{7}{12} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{5}{12} = \frac{7}{24} + \frac{5}{24} = \frac{12}{24} = \frac{1}{2}\). Hence the probability that the second ball is red is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

If \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) then every outcome of \(A\) lies in \(B\), so \(A \cap B = A\) and \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\). Therefore \(P(B|A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)} = \frac{P(A)}{P(A)} = 1\), which is defined since \(P(A) \neq 0\). Hence \(P(B|A) = 1\).
If \(A \cap B = \phi\) then \(P(A \cap B) = 0\). Therefore \(P(B|A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)} = \frac{0}{P(A)} = 0\), which is defined since \(P(A) \neq 0\). Hence \(P(B|A) = 0\).

Writing each outcome as (elder, younger) with \(m\) for male and \(f\) for female, the sample space is \(\{(m,m),(m,f),(f,m),(f,f)\}\), all equally likely. The conditioning event 'at least one male' is \(\{(m,m),(m,f),(f,m)\}\), of probability \(\frac{3}{4}\), and 'both male' is \(\{(m,m)\}\), of probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). The required conditional probability is \(\frac{1/4}{3/4} = \frac{1}{3}\). Hence the answer is \(\frac{1}{3}\).

With outcomes written as (elder, younger), the sample space is \(\{(m,m),(m,f),(f,m),(f,f)\}\). The conditioning event 'the elder child is female' is \(\{(f,m),(f,f)\}\), of probability \(\frac{2}{4}\), and 'both female' is \(\{(f,f)\}\), of probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). The required conditional probability is \(\frac{1/4}{2/4} = \frac{1}{2}\). Hence the answer is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

A leap year has \(366\) days, that is \(52\) complete weeks and \(2\) extra days. The \(52\) weeks already supply \(52\) Tuesdays, so a \(53\)rd Tuesday occurs exactly when one of the two extra days is a Tuesday. The two extra days are consecutive, and the equally likely possibilities are \(\{\)Sun, Mon\(\}\), \(\{\)Mon, Tue\(\}\), \(\{\)Tue, Wed\(\}\), \(\{\)Wed, Thu\(\}\), \(\{\)Thu, Fri\(\}\), \(\{\)Fri, Sat\(\}\), \(\{\)Sat, Sun\(\}\), so the sample space has \(7\) outcomes. Exactly \(2\) of them contain a Tuesday. Hence the required probability is \(\frac{2}{7}\).

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be the events that subsystem A fails and subsystem B fails. 'B fails alone' means B fails and A does not, so \(P(B) = P(B \text{ alone}) + P(A \cap B) = 0.15 + 0.15 = 0.30\). Therefore \(P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{0.15}{0.30} = 0.5\). Hence \(P(A \text{ fails} \mid B \text{ has failed}) = 0.5\).

'A fails alone' means A fails while B does not, so its probability is \(P(A) - P(A \cap B)\). Substituting \(P(A) = 0.2\) and \(P(A \cap B) = 0.15\) gives \(0.2 - 0.15 = 0.05\). Hence \(P(A \text{ fails alone}) = 0.05\).
